stem: In which order are these processes carried out when making peanut butter?

options.content: Shelling, roasting, grinding, packaging
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Roasting, shelling, packaging, grinding
options.rationale: The pods are shelled first, and the product is packaged last.

options.content: Grinding, shelling, roasting, packaging
options.rationale: The kernels must be shelled and roasted before grinding.

options.content: Shelling, grinding, roasting, packaging
options.rationale: The kernels are roasted before they are ground.

explanation: The pods are shelled, the kernels sorted and roasted, the skins removed, the kernels ground into a paste and the paste packaged.

stem: What is meant by value addition?

options.content: Processing a raw product into a product of higher value
options.rationale: Correct: for example, turning groundnuts into peanut butter.

options.content: Selling a raw product at the highest possible price
options.rationale: Value addition changes the product itself.

options.content: Adding salt to a product to make it heavier
options.rationale: Salt is added for flavour, and this is not the meaning of value addition.

options.content: Growing more of a crop on the same land
options.rationale: That is increasing the yield, not adding value.

explanation: Value addition is processing a raw product into one that is worth more, keeps longer and creates work, such as making peanut butter from groundnuts.

stem: What term describes processing a raw product, such as groundnuts, into a product of higher value, such as peanut butter?
explanation: Value addition.

stem: Why are shelled groundnuts roasted before they are ground into peanut butter?

options.content: To develop the flavour and colour, drive off moisture and loosen the skins
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To remove the shells from the kernels
options.rationale: The shells are removed before roasting.

options.content: To turn the kernels into oil
options.rationale: Grinding releases the oil; roasting does not turn kernels into oil.

options.content: To make the kernels heavier
options.rationale: Roasting drives off water, so the kernels become lighter.

explanation: Roasting develops the roasted flavour and brown colour, drives off moisture so the nuts grind easily and keep well, loosens the skins and kills many microorganisms.

stem: Which piece of equipment is used to separate loosened skins from roasted groundnut kernels?

options.content: A winnowing basket
options.rationale: Correct: the light skins are blown away in a breeze.

options.content: A mortar and pestle
options.rationale: This is used for grinding.

options.content: A groundnut sheller
options.rationale: This removes the pods, not the thin skins.

options.content: A screw press
options.rationale: This is used to press oil out of peanut butter.

explanation: In a winnowing basket the light skins are blown away while the heavier kernels fall back.

stem: A worker tosses a mixture of groundnut kernels and pieces of shell in a winnowing basket in a breeze. Why does this separate them?

options.content: The light pieces of shell are blown away, while the heavier kernels fall back into the basket.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The kernels dissolve in the air, leaving the shells behind.
options.rationale: Solids do not dissolve in air.

options.content: The shells are magnetic and stick to the basket.
options.rationale: Shells are not magnetic.

options.content: The kernels are blown away and the shells stay in the basket.
options.rationale: This is the wrong way round: the shells are lighter.

explanation: Winnowing separates materials by how easily they are carried by moving air: light shells and skins are blown aside, heavier kernels drop straight back.

stem: Why must mouldy groundnut kernels be removed before roasting?

options.content: They may contain aflatoxins, poisons that roasting does not destroy completely.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: They make the roaster dirty.
options.rationale: The real problem is the poison in the nuts.

options.content: Mouldy kernels burn and set the roaster on fire.
options.rationale: This is not the reason.

options.content: Mould turns the peanut butter a lighter colour.
options.rationale: The danger is to health, not to the colour.

explanation: Moulds on damp or damaged groundnuts can make aflatoxins, which damage the liver. Roasting does not remove them completely, so the kernels must be sorted out before processing.
hints: Does heating always make a poisonous substance safe?

stem: Roasting groundnuts is a physical change.
explanation: False. Roasting forms new substances that give the brown colour and roasted flavour, and it cannot be reversed, so it is a chemical change.

stem: Grinding roasted groundnuts into peanut butter is a physical change.
explanation: True. Grinding breaks the kernels into small particles and releases their oil, but no new substance is formed.

stem: Peanut butter is sealed in airtight jars. Which of these are reasons for this? Select all that apply.

options.content: To keep out oxygen, which makes the oil go rancid
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To keep out moisture, so that moulds cannot grow
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To keep out dust and insects
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: To make the peanut butter heavier
options.rationale: Sealing a jar does not change the mass of the peanut butter.

options.content: To make the oil separate out faster
options.rationale: Sealing does not speed up oil separation.

options.content: To add protein to the peanut butter
options.rationale: Packaging adds nothing to the food.

explanation: Airtight packaging keeps out the oxygen that makes oil rancid, the moisture that lets moulds grow, and dust and insects.

stem: Match each stage of making peanut butter with its purpose.

right.content: Develops flavour and colour and loosens the skins
Breaks the kernels into a paste and releases the oil
Keeps the product clean and fresh
Removes the kernels from the pods
Removes stones and mouldy or damaged kernels

explanation: Each stage has one main job: shell, sort, roast, grind, pack.

stem: A farmer shells 50 kg of groundnuts in their pods and obtains 34 kg of kernels. What percentage of the mass of the pods is kernel?
explanation: Shelling percentage = 34 ÷ 50 × 100% = 68%.

stem: A club makes 15 kg of peanut butter and fills it into jars that each hold 250 g. How many jars can it fill?
hints: Convert kilograms to grams first: 1 kg = 1000 g.

stem: A school club buys $30\ \text{kg}$ of shelled groundnuts at \$1.20 per kilogram. It spends \$9.00 on firewood and salt, and \$0.35 on each of the 70 jars it fills. It sells all 70 jars at \$1.50 each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total cost of making the peanut butter, in dollars.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the income from selling the jars, in dollars.

explanation: Total cost = \$36.00 (nuts) + \$9.00 (firewood and salt) + \$24.50 (jars) = \$69.50. Income = \$105.00. Profit = \$35.50.
hints: Add up every cost: groundnuts, firewood and salt, and jars.

stem: A jar of peanut butter without stabiliser is left standing for several weeks, and a layer of oil collects on top. Why does the oil rise to the top?

options.content: The oil is less dense than the solid particles.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The oil evaporates and condenses on the surface.
options.rationale: The oil does not evaporate at room temperature.

options.content: The oil is denser than the solid particles.
options.rationale: A denser liquid would sink, not rise.

options.content: Air in the jar pulls the oil upwards.
options.rationale: Air does not pull the oil up; the less dense oil floats.

explanation: The oil is less dense than the crushed solids, so it slowly separates and floats to the top.

stem: Why is peanut butter warmed slightly before it is pressed to extract oil?

options.content: Warm oil is runnier, so it flows out through the cloth more easily.
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Warming turns the protein into oil.
options.rationale: Heating does not turn protein into oil.

options.content: Warming kills the aflatoxins.
options.rationale: Aflatoxins are not destroyed completely by heat, and that is not why it is warmed.

options.content: Warming makes the peanut butter set hard.
options.rationale: Warming makes it softer and runnier.

explanation: Oil flows more easily when warm (it is less viscous), so more of it is squeezed out through the cloth in the same time.
hints: Think about how cooking oil pours on a cold morning compared with a hot day.

stem: After oil has been pressed out of peanut butter, a solid is left in the cloth bag. What is it called, and what is it mainly used for?

options.content: Groundnut cake, used as a protein-rich animal feed
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Groundnut shells, used as firewood
options.rationale: The shells were removed before roasting.

options.content: Slag, used to build roads
options.rationale: Slag comes from the blast furnace.

options.content: Margarine, used as a spread
options.rationale: Margarine is made from the oil, not from the solid.

explanation: The solid left is groundnut cake. It is rich in protein and is used in animal feed and as food.

stem: Which use of peanut oil depends on a chemical reaction between the oil and an alkali such as sodium hydroxide?

options.content: Making soap
options.rationale: Correct: oils and fats react with alkalis to form soap.

options.content: Frying food
options.rationale: Frying uses the oil to transfer heat.

options.content: Burning in a lamp
options.rationale: This is combustion with oxygen, not a reaction with an alkali.

options.content: Rubbing on the skin as a lotion
options.rationale: No reaction with an alkali takes place.

explanation: Boiling an oil with an alkali such as sodium hydroxide makes soap (saponification).
hints: Which product in the chemistry syllabus is made from oils or fats and an alkali?

stem: A processor presses 8.0 kg of peanut butter and collects 1.8 kg of oil. What percentage of the mass of the peanut butter was obtained as oil?
hints: Percentage = mass of oil ÷ mass of peanut butter × 100%.

stem: A women's co-operative in Mutoko wants to make peanut butter from its groundnut harvest.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Outline the stages in making peanut butter from groundnuts in their pods.

points.description: Shell the pods (by hand or with a sheller) and winnow away the shells
Sort out stones and mouldy or damaged kernels
Roast the kernels until golden-brown, then cool them and rub off and winnow away the skins
Grind the kernels into a paste (adding a little salt) and package it in clean, airtight, labelled jars

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name two pieces of equipment that could be used to grind the roasted kernels.

points.description: Peanut butter making machine (mill), or grinding stone (guyo/imbokodo)
Mortar and pestle, or the other item from the first point

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give one reason why the workers should cover their hair and wash their hands.

points.description: To stop hair, dirt or pathogens getting into the food (food hygiene)

explanation: Shell, winnow, sort, roast, cool and remove skins, grind with salt, then package airtight with a label. Grinding equipment: machine, grinding stone, mortar and pestle. Hygiene stops contamination.
hints: Start from the pods and end with the jar on the shelf.
Think of both modern and traditional grinding equipment.

stem: The co-operative also wants to sell peanut oil.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Outline how oil can be obtained by pressing peanut butter.

points.description: Warm the peanut butter slightly so the oil flows easily
Put it in a strong cloth bag in a (screw or lever) press
Squeeze: oil passes through the cloth into a container and the solid cake stays in the bag

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The oil collected is cloudy. Suggest how clear oil can be obtained from it.

points.description: Leave it to stand so solid particles settle, then decant (pour off) or filter the clear oil

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State two uses of peanut oil.

points.description: Cooking or frying, or making margarine
Making soap, or skin creams and hair oils, or lamp fuel

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State one use of the solid left after pressing.

points.description: Animal feed (it is rich in protein), or food

explanation: Warm, bag and press the peanut butter; let the oil settle and decant or filter it. The oil is used for cooking, margarine, soap and cosmetics; the cake is used as animal feed.
hints: The cloth bag acts like a filter.
